title: Hour of AI 2026 - Adaptive
objective: Steer AI toward an intended design by writing specific prompts and refining them based on what comes back. Judge AI output against your own intent, and decide when to accept, redirect, or override it. Use the vocabulary of web design (hero, feature cards, interactive canvas, call-to-action) to analyze what makes a page effective and to describe what you want built. Describe a problem with enough context for AI to give a useful explanation and fix. Verify an AI-proposed fix before trusting it, confirming the problem is resolved and nothing new broke.

project.description: Work on your final project here!

build.title: Build with AI
build.description: Steering AI toward what you intend, and deciding what to do with what comes back.

evidenceLevels.0: Writes vague one-line prompts with no goal, constraint or edge case, accepts whatever comes back, and cannot say why a prompt produced its result.
evidenceLevels.1: States a basic goal in the prompt, notices obvious mismatches with intent when they are visible or pointed out, and revises broadly, asking the AI to fix it or make it better.
evidenceLevels.2: Names a goal, a constraint and an edge case before generating, compares the output against intent to find specific matches and mismatches, and revises by naming the exact element or behavior to change, explaining why the prompt produced what it did.

language.title: Language of web dev
language.description: Naming the parts of a page and understanding how they work.

evidenceLevels.0: Sees a site as one flat idea; sketches are decorative rather than structural, and recurring components go unrecognized even when pointed out.
evidenceLevels.1: Identifies basic components such as the nav bar, hero, cards and footer in an existing page when prompted, and fills in a heavily scaffolded wireframe or site map with inconsistent structure and no clear hierarchy.
evidenceLevels.2: Breaks a multi-page product into pages and components with a clear hierarchy, strips detail away to show structure only and can say why, and lays out a site map or wireframe that supports a plausible user flow with patterns applied consistently.
evidenceLevels.3: Anticipates navigation needs the task did not spell out, moves between site map and wireframe as a decision requires, and picks or adapts a layout pattern on purpose rather than defaulting to the first idea.

debug.title: Debug with AI
debug.description: Describing a problem so AI can help, and checking that the fix worked.

evidenceLevels.0: Avoids or dismisses error messages, cannot pick out the relevant part of one, and pastes whole code or applies any suggested fix without understanding it.
evidenceLevels.1: Reads an error when prompted but treats it as a stop sign, identifies the literal text without connecting it to the code, and pastes it to the AI with no context.
evidenceLevels.2: Treats an error as the start of a diagnosis, connects it to the line or element at fault and restates it in their own words, and gives the AI the error plus the intended behavior and what changed.
evidenceLevels.3: Tests deliberately to surface errors as feedback, predicts likely causes from prior bugs before reading the full message, and fixes the bug from the AI's explanation, asking for a direct patch only as a check.

checkpoints.title: Intro
checkpoints.description: Intro panels

plan.template: Build me a site about {topic} for {audience} that should feel {style}. What it should do: {purpose}

panels.text: ###Dream it. Describe it. Build it.

###Start with a vision. 
Who needs something, and what would you make for them? You’ll pick up the language of web developers as you build with AI.

###Spark your ideas.
Check out these examples then think about what YOU want to build!

####Build it!
In this lesson, your path is unique. Share your idea and your coding experience, and your lesson shifts with every answer along the way.

steps.title: What are you into?
steps.description: Pick one, or type your own.

choices.text: Music and art
Sports and fitness
Food and cooking
Gaming
School and education
Animals and nature
Fashion and style
Friends and community
Share a message
Help them decide or plan
Bring people together
Let them play or try something
My friends and family
My class or school
People into the same topic
My team or club
Just me
Calm and clean
Bold and energetic
Playful and fun
Cozy and friendly

steps.title: Your plan
steps.description: Build a first version with AI, or start from a blank page.

steps.title: Your starter site
steps.instructions: This is your site. Look it over, change anything you like, then continue.
steps.projectPrompt: The first version of the student's website, built from their plan: a hero with a headline that says what the site is for, one or two sections that fit the topic, and a call-to-action. Keep the look and feel simple, but appropriate for their given topic. It should feel clean but not overly polished.

checkpoints.title: Skill Check
checkpoints.description: A few quick questions to find your starting point. Not graded.

steps.title: Your experience
steps.description: Pick the closest one. These questions find your starting point. They are not graded.

questions.questionTitle: Have you worked on a website before?

choices.text: No, this is new to me
I have used a website builder or a template
I have changed code (HTML, CSS or JavaScript) before
I have built websites on my own

questions.questionTitle: Which sentence sounds most like you?

choices.text: I’m new to this. I haven’t worked with website code before.
I know some of the basics, like headings, buttons, and links that make up a page.
I can describe how a page looks, like its colors, fonts, and layout.
I can describe how a page behaves, like what happens when someone clicks or types.

questions.questionTitle: You want a button that changes color when someone clicks it. Which instruction would work best?

choices.text: Style the button with a blue background color.
Add a click event that changes the button’s color.
Make the button look better and work better.
Add a button element that says “Click me.”
I’m not sure.

questions.questionTitle: You want a page with a heading and three cards in a row. Which instruction would work best?

choices.text: Add a heading and three cards.
Add an h1 and three div elements.
Add an h1, then place three cards side by side.
Use flexbox to lay out three card divs in a row.
I’m not sure.

questions.questionTitle:
Your heading looks wrong, and everything after it is huge too. You open the code and see this:

Panda Fan Club

Welcome to the club!

Which instruction to the AI would work best?

choices.text: It’s broken. Fix it.
Add a CSS rule to fix the heading color.
Update the click handler so the heading changes.
Close the h1 tag after “Panda Fan Club”.
I’m not sure.

checkpoints.title: Steer It
checkpoints.description: Writes a prompt with 2 or more specific details, or a follow-up that changes one thing.

panels.text:
**A vague idea leads to a generic page.**

---
Prompt: “Make a website.”

**Specific prompts create the page you pictured.**

----

Prompt: “Make a blue skate park page.”

**Add details to make your vision clearer.**

---

Prompt: “Enlarge the ramp image and pink button.”

steps.title: Steer your first version

validation.condition: The project changed to match a prompt with two or more specific details, or a follow-up that changed one thing.

steps.instructionsPrompt:
Task: In their own project, write a follow-up prompt that adds details or changes one thing.
Outline: Prompt: "What would you change first? Add a detail or change one thing, and say what to keep." The tutor reads the prompt.
Evidence: a prompt with 2 or more specific details, or a follow-up that changes one thing.

checkpoints.title: Use the Lingo
checkpoints.description: Names a block of their page and what it is for.

panels.text:
###Sections of a webpage

When you name the section you want to work on it makes it easier to build with AI.

###Hero Banner

The **hero** section introduces your page.

###Feature Cards

Smaller 'feature cards' show key info or options.

###Interactive Canvas
An 'interactive canvas' lets users play or create.

###Call-to-action
A 'call-to-action' button guides you to the next step.

steps.title: Name a block in your project

validation.condition: A prompt asked for a change by naming one part of the page and saying what that part is for.

steps.instructionsPrompt:
Task: Ask the AI for a change that names one block of their page and says what it is for.
Outline: Prompt: "Pick one part of your page and ask for a change. Name it and say its job."
Evidence: a prompt that names a block and its job.

checkpoints.title: Keep or Redirect
checkpoints.description: Compares what came back with a plan and decides: keep, redirect or edit.

panels.text:
###Start with a plan.

Decide who your page is for, what belongs on it, and what visitors should be able to do.

####Compare the result to your plan.

Check the content, layout, and features. What matches? What’s missing or different?

###Keep what works.

If the page meets your goals and works when you test it, you can keep it as is.

####You decide what to keep!

Write a new prompt that explains what missed the mark, what to change, and what to keep.

steps.title: Decide on a real change
steps.instructionsPrompt:
Task: Write a one-sentence plan for a part of their page, then decide what to do when the AI changes it.
Outline: First the student writes a one-sentence plan, such as "A friendly headline and the blue button." When the AI changes something, the tutor shows the plan beside the result and asks: "Does this match? Keep it, redirect it or edit it, and say why."
Evidence: a decision with a reason that refers to the plan.

checkpoints.title: Give Context
checkpoints.description: Reports a problem with what was expected, what happened and where.

panels.imageUrl: https://images.code.org/fcfe80dab9c17c530f44230ca8fda3ff-Frustrated student faces a broken bakery gallery.png
panels.text:
###“It’s not working.”
Mateo is building a website for his parents’ bakery, but the photos overlap. He tells AI, “It’s not working. Fix it.” After another try, the problem is still there.

panels.imageUrl: https://images.code.org/c71394dfc04d1e494e3bac2d9785a58c-Imagined bakery site in a thought bubble.png
panels.text:
###Get specific.
He tries again: “In the photo gallery, the pictures overlap. I want three equal-sized photos in one row, with space between them.”

###Find the pattern.
Mateo checks the updated page. It works! He notices what helped: name the part, describe what happens, and explain what should happen. Then test the change.

steps.title: Report a problem in your project
steps.instructionsPrompt:
Task: When something breaks or looks wrong, report what they expected, what happened and where.
Outline: Needs a real problem. Prompt: "Tell the AI what you expected, what happened and where." If nothing breaks, the tutor may offer a safe problem (parked for engineering).
Evidence: what was expected, what happened and where, all in one message.

checkpoints.title: Check the Fix
checkpoints.description: Checks that a fix worked and that nothing new broke.

panels.text: After a fix, reload the page to see if the changes worked.
Click on every button and link. Make sure all interactive elements still work.
Carefully check the entire page for any new problems or broken parts.

questions.questionTitle: The AI says it fixed your broken button. You reload the page and the button works. Which two things should you do next?

choices.text: Move on, since the button works now.
Click through the rest of the page.
Ask the AI to confirm that everything works.
Look for anything that changed or broke.
Start over from your first version.
Both B and D
Both A and D

steps.title: Check your fix
steps.instructionsPrompt:
Task: After the AI offers a fix, check that the problem is gone and nothing new broke.
Outline: Prompt: "How did you check? Say what you tried."
Evidence: a stated check, such as "I reloaded and the image appears."

checkpoints.title: A list and a random pick
checkpoints.description: Describes a list of options and a random pick, using list and pick words, so the page chooses one by chance.

panels.text:
###A list holds the options.
Ask AI to store your lunch choices in a **list**, so your website can use them.

####A random pick chooses one by chance.
Ask AI to make the button randomly select one item from your list when clicked.

####An animation shows the action.
Ask AI to add a spinning animation that ends on the selected item. The random pick decides the result; the animation reveals it.

steps.title: Describe your list and your pick

validation.condition: The student told the AI what the options are and that the page picks one of them from the list by chance.

steps.instructionsPrompt:
Task: Tell the AI what the options are and how the page should pick one.
Outline: Prompt: "What are your options, and how should the page choose one?"
Evidence: explains that the page picks one item from a list by chance.

checkpoints.title: A number and a rule
checkpoints.description: Describes a number that changes and a rule that uses it.

panels.text:
### Keep track of the score.
A **variable** stores the score. Collecting a jewel adds one point.

### Check a condition.
A **condition** checks whether something is true, like “Has the score reached 10?”

### Give the rule an action.
If the score reaches 10, end the round. Tell AI both the **condition** and what happens next.

questions.questionTitle: A rule tells a program what to do when something happens. Which of these sentences describes a 'rule' that dictates what happens on a web page?

choices.text: The score is 7.
If the score reaches 10, the round ends.
The button is blue.
The page has a title.

questions.text: You just identified what a 'rule' looks like. Now, think about your own page. What's one thing you want to happen only if a certain condition is met? Write that rule using 'if... then...' phrasing.
questions.placeholder: For example: If the button is clicked, then show a message.

steps.title: Add a number and a rule
steps.instructionsPrompt:
Task: Ask the AI for a number that changes (score, count or lives) and a rule that uses it.
Outline: Prompt: "What number will change, and what rule will use it?" The tutor shows the rule they wrote.
Evidence: names the number that changes and the rule that uses it.

checkpoints.title: Remember and show
checkpoints.description: Describes what the page should remember and what should show on screen.

panels.text:
### A page can remember a choice.
Ask AI to **save** what a visitor picks, so your page can use it again.

### A click can save a pick.
A **call-to-action** tells visitors what to do next. This button saves their choice.

### Show the saved choice.
Ask AI to display the saved pick as a **preview**, so visitors can see what they chose.

### Make results easy to read.
Show saved choices as **bars, counts, or previews**. Tell AI which display fits your page.

steps.title: Remember and show in your project

validation.condition: The student told the AI what the page should remember and what should change on screen when it does.

steps.instructionsPrompt:
Task: Tell the AI what the page should remember and what should show right away.
Outline: Prompt: "What should your page remember, and what should show when it does?"
Evidence: names what is remembered and what changes on screen.

checkpoints.title: Layout and spacing
checkpoints.description: Uses layout words and block names to describe space, alignment and order.

panels.text:
### Crowded?
When everything competes for attention, it’s hard to know where to look.

### Give each part room.
Ask AI to add **spacing** so each section is easier to scan.

### Guide the eye.
Put the main idea first. Use **order** to lead visitors toward the next step.
Order guides the eye.

questions.questionTitle: Your club page has three cards that feel crowded. Which prompt is most likely to fix the problem?

choices.text: Make the cards look more polished and modern overall.
Give each card a different color so they stand out more.
Add more space between the three cards.
Make the text on each card bigger so it is easier to read.

steps.title: Describe a layout change

validation.condition: A prompt named the blocks that need more room or a different order and said how they should be arranged.

steps.instructionsPrompt:
Task: Ask the AI for a layout change that names the blocks and how they should be arranged.
Outline: Prompt: "Which blocks need more room or a different order? Say how they should be arranged."
Evidence: a prompt that names blocks and says how they should be arranged.

checkpoints.title: Style and consistency
checkpoints.description: Names a style in words and restates it across changes so the AI keeps it steady.

panels.text:
###You started with a clear style.

Repeated colors, shapes, and spacing help your page feel planned.

###Watch for style drift.
A change can clash with the style you started with.

###Small changes add up.
Different buttons, colors, and shapes can make the page feel unplanned.

###Name your style.
Tell AI: “Use blue tones, rounded shapes, and generous spacing.”

###Repeat it with each change.
Include your style in new prompts. Check that AI’s changes still match.

questions.text:
You just learned the importance of naming your site's style to maintain consistency. Now, consider your own project!
1. In three words, describe its overall visual style.

    - *For example, you might choose words like 'calm, clean, rounded'.*

2. Explain how you plan to implement the style across your page.
questions.placeholder: Enter three words to describe your site's style.

steps.title: Keep your style across two changes
steps.instructionsPrompt:
Task: Make two more changes to their project and restate the style each time.
Outline: Prompt: "Make your next change and say your style again." The tutor checks a second change too.
Evidence: a follow-up that restates the style while changing one thing.

checkpoints.title: Readable and clear
checkpoints.description: Asks for text size, contrast and wording that make a block easy to read.

panels.text:
### Make it readable.
Ask AI to increase the **text size** so visitors can read comfortably.

### Help text stand out.
Use strong **contrast** between text and its background.

### Keep wording simple.
“Sign up for a hike” is clearer than “Utilize the registration portal.”

steps.title: Ask for a readability change

validation.condition: A prompt named a block that is hard to read and asked for a size, contrast or wording change to it.

steps.instructionsPrompt:
Task: Pick a block that is hard to read and ask for a size, contrast or wording change.
Outline: Prompt: "Which block is hardest to read? Ask for a change."
Evidence: a prompt that names a block and a readability change.

checkpoints.title: Say it in your voice
checkpoints.description: Names a tone in words and restates it across changes so the AI keeps it steady.

panels.text:
### Make it playful.
“Your next favorite band is waiting.” Ask AI for a **playful tone**.

### Keep it calm.
“Take a break. Discover some live music.”

Ask for a **calm tone**.

### Go bold.
“Make some noise. Find your next show.”

Ask for a **bold tone**.

### Keep the voice consistent.
Name your **tone**, then check that AI carries it through the page.

steps.title: Your site's tone in three words

questions.text:
You just learned how important tone words are for keeping your site consistent. Now, think about your own project:

**In three words, how should your site sound to visitors?**

*For example, you might choose words like 'friendly, calm, or funny'.*

steps.title: Keep your tone across two changes
steps.instructionsPrompt:
Task: Make two more changes and restate the tone each time.
Outline: Prompt: "Make your next change and say your tone again."
Evidence: a follow-up that restates the tone while changing one thing.

checkpoints.title: Lead with the point
checkpoints.description: Uses headline words to say what the site is for in the first line.

steps.title: Say it in the first line

panels.text:
###What’s this site for?

“Something amazing starts here” sounds exciting, but says little.

###Say it up front.

Try “Fix your bike at our student-run repair café.”

Make the headline specific.

###Then show the next step.
Add key details below the hero.

Follow them with a clear call-to-action.

questions.questionTitle: Which headline best communicates what a website is about to a new student?

choices.text: Welcome!
Find a club that fits you in two minutes.
Our school, our story.
Click here.

steps.title: Rewrite your headline

validation.condition: The headline now says what the site is for, whether a prompt asked for it or the student edited it by hand.

steps.instructionsPrompt:
Task: Ask the AI to change the headline and first line, or edit them by hand.
Outline: Prompt: "What is your site for? Make the headline say it."
Evidence: a prompt or edit that states the site's purpose in the headline.

checkpoints.title: Make the ask clear
checkpoints.description: Writes a call-to-action with a clear verb and next step.

steps.title: A button that says what to do

panels.text:
### What happens next?
“Click here” gives few clues.

A **call-to-action** should name the next step.

### Name the action.
“Find my club” tells visitors what to do and what to expect.

### Put it where it helps.
Place the **call-to-action** where visitors are ready to act.

### Try it on your site.
Choose what visitors should do next.

Ask AI to add a **call-to-action** that clearly names that action.

steps.title: Rewrite your call-to-action

validation.condition: The call-to-action now has a clear verb and a next step, whether a prompt asked for it or the student edited it by hand.

steps.instructionsPrompt:
Task: Ask for a call-to-action with a clear verb and next step, or edit it by hand.
Outline: Prompt: "What should a visitor do next? Make the button say it."
Evidence: a call-to-action with a clear verb and next step.

checkpoints.title: Read the console
checkpoints.description: Reads an error in the console and says where it points, so a problem report has the context the AI needs.

panels.text:
### Meet the console.
The **console** shows messages from your page as it runs. Open it to look for clues.

### Messages mean different things.
Some show information. **Warnings** flag possible issues, and **errors** report something that went wrong.

### An error is a clue.
Read the message for details about the problem. Ask AI to explain it and suggest what to check.

### Start with the message.
An **error message** gives you a clue about what went wrong.

### What does it name?
Look for a named item.

Share the **exact message** with AI.

### Follow the line.
Check the **file and line number**.

The cause may be there or earlier in the code.

steps.title: Read your console
steps.instructionsPrompt:
Task: Open the console in their project and say what an error points to.
Outline: Needs a real error. Prompt: "Open the console. What does the error point to?"
Evidence: says which keyword or line the error points to.

checkpoints.title: Find it in the code
checkpoints.description: Finds the line for a named block and uses its name to say where a change belongs.

panels.text:
### Start with the page.
Pick a section to explore, like the **hero** at the top.

### Find a matching clue.
Look for familiar text or an **identifier**, such as an ID or class.

### Search for it.
Search for that identifier to find code that builds or styles the section.

steps.title: Find a line in your project

validation.condition: The student pointed to the line or rule in the code for a block they named.

steps.instructionsPrompt:
Task: Find the line for one named block in their code.
Outline: Prompt: "Pick a block and find its line in your code."
Evidence: points to the line or rule for a named block.

checkpoints.title: Undo to find the cause
checkpoints.description: Undoes changes one at a time and checks after each, to verify what caused the problem.

panels.text:
### Something broke.
After a change, test your page.

Here, the banner covers part of the button.

### Undo gives you clues.
**Undo one change at a time**, then test again.

When the problem disappears, the change you reversed is a clue.

### Give AI the clue.
**Tell AI:** “Making the banner taller covered the button. Keep the button visible.”

**Test again** after AI makes the change.

questions.questionTitle: You made three changes to your project, and now something isn't working. What's the best first step to find which change caused the problem?

choices.text: Undo all three changes at once.
Undo the newest change, then check if it's fixed.
Undo the oldest change first.
Do nothing and ask the AI for a new page.

questions.text: You just learned that undoing changes one by one helps pinpoint problems. Now, imagine your project has a new bug after several recent changes. Which specific change do you *guess* might have caused the problem, and why?
questions.placeholder: I think [this change] broke it because [reason]...

steps.title: Find the cause in your project
steps.instructionsPrompt:
Task: Undo one change at a time, check after each, and find which one caused the problem.
Outline: Needs a real problem after more than one change. Prompt: "Undo your newest change. Did it fix it?" Repeat until it works.
Evidence: names the change that caused the problem and how they found it.

checkpoints.title: Show it off
checkpoints.description: Looks back at their hour, writes a sentence about their site, and shares it.

panels.text: Remember all the changes you've made? Let's take a look back at your project's journey.
You can use a slider to replay how your web page changed over time, from your first prompt to your latest edits.
Along the way, you earned special badges for mastering new web development skills!
Like the 'Page Namer' badge, for when you first identified a page part by its proper name.
Or the 'Fix Checker' badge, when you successfully confirmed a bug fix!
Your hard work has paid off! Let's review your journey and celebrate your new skills.
See how your prompts grew more detailed and how many tries it took to get your perfect page.
Replay your closeness ratings, showing how well AI results matched your vision every time.
Special badges will light up, recognizing the key moves you've mastered.

questions.text: You've worked hard on your project! Now, write a short description for a share card that explains what your site is, who you made it for, and what part you're proudest of.
questions.placeholder: Describe your site, its audience, and what you're proudest of...

steps.title: Show it off
steps.instructionsPrompt:
Task: Publish the site and copy its link, then share it with the class.
Outline: Project only. The student publishes the site and copies the link, then shares it with the class: present it, post it, or both. The teacher chooses how. The share card from the last step goes with it.
No evidence needed. The teacher view records that it was shared.
